mainTopic: Can a person take the law into his own hands (עָבֵיד אִינִישׁ דִּינָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ)? Proofs on both sides are rejected, and then a new משנה begins about a jug that breaks in the street.
overview: The גמרא continues the argument between רב נחמן, who holds that a person may take the law into his own hands, and רב יהודה, who holds that he must go to בית דין. First it answers the proof from בן בג בג in two ways: he is a lone opinion, or 'break his teeth' means in court, though that second reading has a wording problem. Then the גמרא tries one proof after another from sources about an ox on top of another ox, jugs filling a courtyard, and a נרצע who refuses to leave. Every proof is pushed away, usually by showing that the person acting faced a real loss or had another reason to act. Next come proofs for רב יהודה from a jug in the street, the woman who grabs her husband's attacker, a public road moved to the side of a field, and פאה taken from the wrong side. These are also turned aside: 'stumbled' is said only to match the end of the משנה, she pays only when she had another way to save him, the road rule comes from the problem of a crooked path, and 'both are פאה' only means both are free from מעשר. Finally a new משנה begins, about a jug that breaks in the street and causes someone to slip or get hurt. רב starts to explain that the jug owner is liable only for clothes dirtied by the water, and his statement continues on the next amud.

steps.title: בן בג בג is only a lone opinion
steps.stepSummary: On behalf of רב יהודה, the גמרא answers the proof from בן בג בג. His view is a lone opinion, and the רבנן disagree with him.
steps.simpleTranslation: Keep that proof for yourself! בן בג בג is a lone opinion, and the רבנן disagree with him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back against the proof for רב נחמן. It says the proof only works according to בן בג בג, and he stands alone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof from בן בג בג's words ('break his teeth') is not denied. Instead the גמרא limits it: one תנא's view cannot decide the law when the majority (רבנן) disagree. So רב יהודה can simply side with the רבנן.

keyTerms.meaning: Literally 'with you.' Here it means 'keep it for yourself,' because the proof does not bother us.
The רבנן (the majority of sages) disagree with him

phrases.english: With you?! (Keep it to yourself!)
Ben Bag Bag is an individual opinion,
and the Rabbis disagree with him.

steps.triggerLanguage: עִמָּךְ בֶּן בַּג בַּג יְחִידָאָה הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the proof for רב נחמן from בן בג בג, which was brought just before this section.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Limiting the source to a minority opinion
steps.terutzHavaAmina: בן בג בג's statement seemed to prove that a person may take the law into his own hands.
steps.terutzMaskana: It reflects only a lone view that the רבנן reject, so רב יהודה is not refuted.

steps.title: רבי ינאי: 'Break his teeth' means in court
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי gives a different answer. 'Break his teeth' does not mean physical force. It means beating him in court.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי said: What does 'break his teeth' mean? Through judgment, in court.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי ינאי offers a second way to answer the proof. He reads בן בג בג's words as a figure of speech for winning in court.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first answer said בן בג בג disagrees with רב יהודה. רבי ינאי says there is no disagreement at all. Read this way, בן בג בג is also telling you to go to בית דין and not to grab the item yourself.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai says:
What does 'break his teeth' mean? In judgment.
phrases.notes: 'Break his teeth' is quoted from בן בג בג's statement, which the גמרא brought just before this section.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יַנַּאי אָמַר מַאי שְׁבוֹר אֶת שִׁינָּיו בַּדִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A second, separate answer to the same proof. It reinterprets the source instead of calling it a minority view.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the wording of the source
steps.terutzHavaAmina: 'Break his teeth' sounds like using force yourself.
steps.terutzMaskana: It means defeating him through בית דין, which fits רב יהודה.

steps.title: The wording doesn't fit רבי ינאי's reading
steps.stepSummary: If court action is meant, the ברייתא should have said 'they (the court) say to him' and 'he is taking what is his.' This problem is left unanswered.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does it say 'and say to him'? It should have said 'and they say to him'! Why 'I am taking what is mine'? It should have said 'he is taking what is his'! This is a difficulty.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks רבי ינאי's reading from the wording of the ברייתא itself. It ends with 'קשיא,' meaning no answer was found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If בית דין does the 'breaking,' then בית דין should be the one speaking. That would call for third-person wording ('they say,' 'his'). The ברייתא uses first person ('say,' 'mine'), which shows the owner himself acts and speaks. So רבי ינאי's answer is weakened, though the first answer (lone opinion) still stands.
steps.confusionAlert: 'קשיא' here does not overturn רב יהודה's whole position. It only knocks out רבי ינאי's reading. The first answer, that בן בג בג is a lone opinion, still works.

phrases.english: If so, 'and say to him'?!
It should have said 'and they say to him'!
phrases.notes: 'They' would be the judges. If the court is acting, the court should be the one talking.

phrases.english: 'I am taking what is mine'?!
It should have said 'he is taking what is his'!
It is difficult.

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי וֶאֱמוֹר לוֹ וְאוֹמְרִים לוֹ מִיבְּעֵי לֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי ינאי's reading from step 2.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי ינאי's reading of 'break his teeth' as court action
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The first-person wording ('say,' 'mine') shows the owner acts himself, not the court.

steps.title: New proof for רב נחמן: the ox on top
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: one ox climbed on another to kill it. The bottom ox's owner pulled his ox away, and the top ox fell and died. He is exempt. The גמרא suggests this case is about a מועד, where he would have been fully paid anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: An ox climbed on top of another ox to kill it. The owner of the bottom ox came and pulled his ox away. The top ox fell and died. He is exempt. Isn't this talking about a מועד ox, where there is no loss?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof for רב נחמן, that a person may take the law into his own hands. It ends by suggesting how to read the case. Watch for a possible rejection next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the attacking ox is a מועד, its owner pays full damages. So the bottom ox's owner would lose nothing by waiting for court. Even so, he is exempt for saving his ox himself. That suggests a person may act on his own even when court would have made him whole, which is רב נחמן's view.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox known to gore. Its owner pays full damages.

steps.whyThisMatters: This case tests whether self-help is allowed even when there is no financial need for it. That is exactly where רב יהודה and רב נחמן split.

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: שׁוֹר שֶׁעָלָה עַל גַּבֵּי חֲבֵירוֹ לְהוֹרְגוֹ,
phrases.english: An ox that climbed onto the back of another to kill it,

phrases.aramaic: וּבָא בַּעַל הַתַּחְתּוֹן וְשָׁמַט אֶת שֶׁלּוֹ,
phrases.english: and the owner of the bottom one came and pulled his away,
and the top one fell and died: he is exempt.
What, is it not about a forewarned ox,
where there is no loss?
phrases.notes: No loss because the owner of a מועד pays in full. Waiting for בית דין would have cost him nothing.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע שׁוֹר שֶׁעָלָה עַל גַּבֵּי חֲבֵירוֹ לְהוֹרְגוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the בן בג בג proof was answered, the גמרא tries a new source for רב נחמן.
steps.raayaObject: רב נחמן's view that a person may take the law into his own hands
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא exempting the bottom ox's owner when he pulls his ox away and the attacker dies, read as a case of a מועד

steps.title: The ox case may be about a תם, where there is a loss
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the proof. The attacking ox may be a תם, and then the bottom ox's owner would really lose money, so he is allowed to act.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. The case is about a תם, where there is a loss.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes away the proof from the two oxen. It says the attacking ox could be a תם, not a מועד.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner of a תם pays only half the damage. So if the bottom ox were killed, its owner would lose the other half. That means he acted to prevent a real loss, and the case proves nothing about acting when there is no loss.

keyTerms.meaning: An ox that has not yet become known as an attacker. Its owner pays only half the damage.
No. This opens a rejection of the proof.

phrases.english: No, it is about a תם
phrases.notes: He means the ox on top, the one attacking.

phrases.english: where there is a loss.
phrases.notes: The loss belongs to the owner of the bottom ox, since he would only get half his damage back.

steps.triggerLanguage: לָא, בְּתָם – דְּאִיכָּא פְּסֵידָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of step 4 by reading the case differently.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the proof. It does not prove the opposite view.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the ox was a מועד. If it is a תם, there is a real loss, so the case does not show that one may act when there is no loss.

steps.title: The end of the ברייתא makes a תם reading difficult
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the תם reading. The end of the ברייתא says that if he pushed the top ox and it died, he is liable. But if it is a תם and he faces a loss, why should he be liable?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, look at the end of the ברייתא: if he pushed the top ox and it died, he is liable. And if it is a תם, why is he liable?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the new reading from step 5 using the last part of the same ברייתא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the case is a תם, the bottom ox's owner is protecting himself from a real loss, so he should be allowed to act. Yet the סיפא makes him liable for pushing the top ox. That seems to fit better with a מועד, where he had no loss and no right to act.

keyTerms.meaning: If so. This opens a challenge to what was just said.
The last part of a משנה or ברייתא

phrases.english: If so, say the last part:
if he pushed the top one and it died, he is liable.
And if it is about a תם, why is he liable?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אֵימָא סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the תם reading given in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in step 5 that the ברייתא is about a תם.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: With a תם there is a real loss, and a person may act to prevent a loss. So the ruling of liability in the סיפא does not seem to fit.

steps.title: He is liable because he could have just pulled his ox away
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers: he is liable because he should have pulled his own ox out, and he did not. He chose the more harmful way.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because he should have pulled his ox away, and he did not pull it away.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge and keeps the תם reading.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even when a person is allowed to protect himself, he must use the least harmful way. Pulling his own ox away would have saved it without hurting the other ox. Since he pushed the attacker and killed it instead, he must pay.

keyTerms.meaning: To pull it away, meaning to pull his own ox out from underneath

steps.whatToRemember: The ox ברייתא proves nothing. It can be about a תם (a real loss), and the liability in the סיפא is because he used a harmful method when a harmless one was available.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows a limit on acting for yourself: even when it is allowed, you may not damage another person's property if you could have protected yourself without doing so.

phrases.english: Because he should have pulled it away,
phrases.notes: "It" is his own ox, the one on the bottom.

phrases.english: and he did not pull it away.

steps.triggerLanguage: שֶׁהָיָה לוֹ לְשׇׁמְטוֹ, וְלֹא שְׁמָטוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 6 and keeps the reading of step 5.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains why he is liable without dropping the תם reading
steps.terutzHavaAmina: If he faces a loss, he may do anything to protect himself, so he should not be liable.
steps.terutzMaskana: He may protect himself, but he is liable if he chose a harmful way when a harmless way (pulling his ox away) was available.

steps.title: New proof: a courtyard filled with jugs
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא. If someone fills his friend's courtyard with jugs of wine and oil, the courtyard owner may break them to go out and to come in.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if someone fills his friend's courtyard with jugs of wine and jugs of oil, the owner of the courtyard may break his way out and break his way in.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new attempt to prove that a person may take the law into his own hands. This sets up the next round of discussion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The courtyard owner is not losing money here; he simply cannot get through. Even so, he may break the jugs on his own, without going to court. That seems to show a person may act for himself even when he faces no loss.

keyTerms.meaning: A person may take the law into his own hands. This is the question the whole discussion is about.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who fills his friend's courtyard
with jugs of wine and jugs of oil,
the owner of the courtyard breaks them and goes out,
breaks them and comes in!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַמְמַלֵּא חֲצַר חֲבֵירוֹ כַּדֵּי יַיִן וְכַדֵּי שֶׁמֶן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The ox proof was pushed away, so the גמרא tries a new source.
steps.raayaObject: The view that a person may take the law into his own hands even when he faces no loss.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא: the owner of the courtyard may break the jugs to go out and come in.

steps.title: Breaking the jugs only to reach court
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק says the courtyard owner may break the jugs only to go out to בית דין or to go in and get his proof documents.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: He breaks the jugs to go out to בית דין, and he breaks them to go in and bring the proof of his rights.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק pushes back on the proof from the jugs ברייתא. He explains that the owner breaks the jugs only so he can go to court or fetch his documents.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא seemed to allow a person to act on his own even when it was not really needed. רב נחמן בר יצחק reads it narrowly: breaking is allowed only to reach בית דין and to bring his proof, because without that he would lose. So the ברייתא does not show that a person may take the law into his own hands beyond that.

keyTerms.meaning: His rights, meaning the proof that the courtyard is his

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
He breaks them and goes out to court,
he breaks them and goes in
to bring his proofs.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק: מְשַׁבֵּר וְיוֹצֵא לְבֵית דִּין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof brought from the jugs ברייתא in step 8.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The jugs ברייתא as a proof that a person may act on his own beyond what he needs to avoid a loss.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The breaking is allowed only to reach court or to fetch proof, so it is a case of real loss and not of taking the law into his own hands.

steps.title: A master pushing out a slave whose time is up
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא: if a נרצע's time is over and he refuses to leave, and his master hurts him while pushing him out, the master is exempt, based on the פסוק "לא תקחו כפר לשוב".
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: From where do we know that a נרצע whose days are over, whose master is pushing him to leave, and the master injured him and wounded him, that the master is exempt? The פסוק says "Do not take ransom… to return". Read it as: do not take ransom for the one who must return.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא to show that a person may use force on his own. A master who wounds his slave while forcing him out is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave's time is up, so he must go home, and the master hurts him while pushing him out. The ברייתא says the master pays nothing, learning this from reading "לא תקחו כפר" together with "לשוב". It looks like the master may act on his own even though he could have gone to בית דין.

keyTerms.meaning: A Hebrew slave whose ear was pierced so he stays on longer

phrases.english: Come and hear:
From where do we know regarding a pierced slave whose days have ended,
and his master is urging him to leave,
and he injured him and made a wound on him,
that he is exempt?
The verse says: "You shall not take ransom" "to return"
do not take ransom for the one who must return!
phrases.notes: The ברייתא reads the two words together: the slave who must go home gets no payment for his injury.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: מִנַּיִין לְנִרְצָע שֶׁכָּלוּ לוֹ יָמָיו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the jugs proof was turned aside, the גמרא tries a new ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That a person may take the law into his own hands even where he would not suffer a loss.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about a נרצע, learned from the פסוק "לא תקחו כפר… לשוב".

steps.title: The case is a slave who steals
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא is talking about a slave who is a thief, so the master would really lose if the slave stayed.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are we dealing with here? With a slave who steals.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the slave proof. It says the ברייתא is about a thieving slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the slave steals, every day he stays costs the master money. So the master is facing a real loss, and that is why he may push him out himself. The ברייתא does not prove that a person may act on his own when there is no loss.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here?
A slave who is a thief

steps.whatToRemember: Both proofs are turned aside the same way. In the jugs case and in the slave case, the person acting on his own faces a real loss, so neither one proves he may act when there is no loss.

phrases.english: With what are we dealing here?
With a slave who is a thief.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכָא בְּמַאי עָסְקִינַן – בְּעַבְדָּא גַּנָּבָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof from the נרצע ברייתא in step 10.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The נרצע ברייתא as a proof for acting on one's own without a loss.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The ברייתא can be about a thieving slave, where the master faces a real loss.

steps.title: Why Would the Slave Only Start Stealing Now?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer of Step 11: if the slave never stole until now, why assume he will steal now?
steps.simpleTranslation: Until now he did not steal, and now suddenly he will steal?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own answer from Step 11, that the slave is a thief. If he was honest all these years, why worry that he will start stealing now?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer in Step 11 needed the master to face a real loss if the slave stayed. But if the slave never stole before, the worry looks made up. So the answer itself now needs support.

phrases.english: Until now he did not steal,
and now he will steal?!

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד הָאִידָּנָא לָא גְּנַב, וְהַשְׁתָּא גָּנֵב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer given in Step 11.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is about a slave who steals.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A slave who never stole before gives no reason to fear that he will start stealing now.

steps.title: Until Now He Feared His Master
steps.stepSummary: Until now the slave was afraid of his master, so he held back. Now that he is free, that fear is gone.
steps.simpleTranslation: Until now the fear of his master was on him. Now he no longer has the fear of his master on him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains why the worry starts only now. The slave's fear of his master kept him from stealing, and that fear ends when he goes free.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The slave was always a thief at heart, but fear held him back. Once his time is up and he is no longer under his master, nothing stops him. So the master really does stand to lose, and the answer of Step 11 stands.

phrases.aramaic: עַד הָאִידָּנָא הֲוָה אֵימְתֵיהּ דְּרַבֵּיהּ עֲלֵיהּ,
phrases.english: Until now the fear of his master was upon him,

phrases.aramaic: הַשְׁתָּא לֵית לֵיהּ אֵימְתָא דְּרַבֵּיהּ עֲלֵיהּ.
phrases.english: now he does not have the fear of his master upon him.

steps.triggerLanguage: עַד הָאִידָּנָא הֲוָה אֵימְתֵיהּ דְּרַבֵּיהּ עֲלֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 12.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Explains the facts of the case: a change in the slave's situation creates the danger.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A slave who never stole before would not steal now.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only fear held him back, and that fear disappears when he goes free.

steps.title: A Second Answer: The Slave Was Given a שפחה כנענית
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן בר יצחק explains the ברייתא differently. The master had given the slave a שפחה כנענית. She was permitted to him until now, but now she is forbidden.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן בר יצחק said: The ברייתא is about a slave whose master gave him a Canaanite maidservant. Until now it was permitted, and now it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן בר יצחק offers a different way to explain why the master may push the slave out. If the slave stays, he will be doing an איסור.
steps.deeperAnalysis: While he was an עבד עברי, the slave was allowed to live with the שפחה כנענית. Once his time ends, she becomes forbidden to him. So when the master pushes him out, he is stopping a sin, not just protecting his own money.
steps.confusionAlert: This is not another proof that a person may take the law into his own hands. Here the master is stopping a forbidden act, which is a different reason for pushing the slave out.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak said:
It is about a slave whose master gave him
a Canaanite maidservant;
until now it was permitted,
and now it is forbidden.
phrases.notes: Now that he is free, staying with her would be an איסור. That is why the master may push him out.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב נַחְמָן בַּר יִצְחָק אָמַר: בְּעֶבֶד שֶׁמָּסַר לוֹ רַבּוֹ שִׁפְחָה כְּנַעֲנִית
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a different answer to the proof of Step 10, alongside the answer of Steps 11-13.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Places the ברייתא in a different case.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The master pushes the slave out only to protect himself from a loss.
steps.terutzMaskana: The master pushes him out to stop a forbidden relationship.

steps.title: A Proof from the Jug in the Street
steps.stepSummary: Our משנה says that someone who stumbles on a jug left in the public domain and breaks it is פטור. That suggests that breaking it on purpose would make him חייב.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: If someone leaves a jug in the public domain, and another person comes, stumbles on it, and breaks it, he is exempt. The reason is that he stumbled on it. But if he broke it on purpose, he is liable!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a proof from our משנה. It tries to show that a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה exempts only someone who stumbled. The גמרא reads this to mean that someone who broke the jug on purpose, even though it was blocking his way, must pay. If so, a person may not break something on his own just because it is in his way.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
One who places a jug in the public domain,
and another comes and stumbles on it
and breaks it – he is exempt.
The reason is that he stumbled on it,
but if he broke it, he is liable!

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הַמַּנִּיחַ אֶת הַכַּד בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the earlier proofs were pushed off, the גמרא tries a new proof, this time for the opposite side.
steps.raayaObject: That a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.raayaSupportSource: Our משנה about the jug in the public domain, read by inference from the word 'stumbled'.

steps.title: Breaking It on Purpose Is Also Exempt
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד in the name of רבא says that breaking the jug on purpose is also פטור. The משנה said 'stumbled' only to set up its second half: if the walker gets hurt, the jug's owner pays only when the walker stumbled.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: The same is true even if he broke it on purpose. The משנה says 'stumbled' only because it wants to teach in the second half: if he got hurt, the owner of the barrel must pay for his damage. That is only when he stumbled. But if he broke it on purpose, the owner does not pay, because he hurt himself. That is why the first half says 'stumbled'.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד rejects the proof. Breaking the jug on purpose is also פטור, so the משנה's word 'stumbled' teaches nothing about taking the law into your own hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word 'stumbled' is really needed for the second half of the משנה. The jug's owner pays for the walker's injury only if he stumbled, not if he broke the jug on purpose and hurt himself in the process. The משנה used the same word in the first half to match, so we cannot learn anything from it there.

keyTerms.meaning: Since, because of (it is said to match something else)
The last part of a משנה or ברייתא
The first part of a משנה or ברייתא

steps.whatToRemember: The proof from the jug falls away. The word 'stumbled' in the first half is there only to match the second half, where it really matters for who pays for the walker's injury.
steps.confusionAlert: Do not think that breaking on purpose makes him pay for the jug. The point is that if he breaks it on purpose and gets hurt, the jug's owner does not pay for his injury.

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
The same law applies even if he broke it on purpose;
and the reason it teaches 'stumbled' –
is because it wants to teach in the last part:

phrases.aramaic: אִם הוּזַּק – בַּעַל חָבִית חַיָּיב בְּנִזְקוֹ,
phrases.english: if he was hurt, the owner of the barrel is liable for his damage,
phrases.notes: The משנה starts by saying 'jug' and here says 'barrel'. It is the same item.

phrases.english: which is only when he stumbled,
but if he broke it on purpose, no,
because he hurt himself;
so it teaches 'stumbled' in the first part as well.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: הוּא הַדִּין אֲפִילּוּ שְׁבָרָהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 15.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Fully cancels the inference from the word 'stumbled' in the first part of the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The word 'stumbled' in the first part is only there to match the second part, so nothing can be learned from it.

steps.title: Proof from the woman who must pay for grabbing the attacker
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: 'וקצתה את כפה' means she pays money. It suggests this is even when she had no other way to save her husband, which would show a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: 'Then you shall cut off her hand' means money. Isn't this talking about a case where she could not save her husband any other way?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new proof that a person may not take the law into his own hands. Even a woman saving her husband has to pay.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא says the woman who grabbed the attacker pays money. The גמרא assumes she had no other way to save her husband, and she still pays. If acting on your own were allowed, she should be exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Then you shall cut off her hand (the פסוק in דברים)
Money: she pays, her hand is not really cut off

steps.confusionAlert: Her hand is not actually cut off. The ברייתא reads the פסוק as a money payment.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
"Then you shall cut off her hand" – this means money.
phrases.notes: דברים 25:12. The פסוק is about a woman who grabs, in a shameful way, the man fighting her husband.

phrases.english: What, is it not
where she is not able to save [her husband]
by some other means?

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: ״וְקַצֹּתָה אֶת כַּפָּהּ״ – מָמוֹן. מַאי, לָאו
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the jug was pushed off, the גמרא tries a new proof on the same question.
steps.raayaObject: That a person may not take the law into his own hands (the view of רב יהודה).
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא on דברים 25:12 saying the woman pays money, read as covering a case where she had no other way to save her husband.

steps.title: She pays only when she had another way
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא pushes off the proof: the ברייתא is talking about a case where she could have saved her husband some other way.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. It is talking about where she could have saved him by other means.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא rejects the proof. She pays only because she had a gentler option and chose this one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she had another way and still did this, she went too far, so of course she pays. That says nothing about a case with no other choice. So the ברייתא does not prove a person can never act on his own.

phrases.english: No,

phrases.aramaic: שֶׁיְּכוֹלָה לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר.
phrases.english: [it is] where she is able to save [him] by other means.

steps.triggerLanguage: לֹא, שֶׁיְּכוֹלָה לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof of Step 17 by narrowing the case.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: Rejects only the assumption about the case. The ruling that she pays still stands.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed she had no other option. The ברייתא can be read as a case where she did have another option.

steps.title: Then why didn't the ברייתא say so in her own case?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. If she is exempt when there was no other way, the ברייתא should have said so right in her case, instead of teaching in its last part that 'ושלחה ידה' leaves out a שליח בית דין.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if she could not save him any other way, she is exempt? If so, instead of teaching at the end that 'And she put out her hand' leaves out a messenger of the court, let it make a split in her own case: when is this said? When she could have saved him another way. But if she could not, she is exempt!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא questions the answer of Step 18. It says the ברייתא's wording does not fit it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The end of the ברייתא learns from 'ושלחה ידה' that a שליח בית דין who does this is פטור. If the woman herself could also be פטור when she had no choice, it would have been simpler to say that directly about her. Since the ברייתא did not say it, maybe she always pays.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of a ברייתא or משנה
A messenger acting on behalf of the court
Let it make a split and teach it
In what case are these words said?

phrases.english: But where she is not able to save [him]
by other means, she is exempt?
If so, instead of teaching in the last part:
"And she put out her hand" –
this leaves out a messenger of the court;
let it make a split and teach it in her own case:
In what case are these words said?

phrases.aramaic: בְּשֶׁיְּכוֹלָה לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר,
phrases.english: Where she is able to save [him] by other means,
but where she is not able to save [him]
by other means, she is exempt!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אַדְּתָנֵי סֵיפָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of Step 18 using the wording of the same ברייתא.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim in Step 18 that she is exempt when she had no other way.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If that split were true, the ברייתא should have stated it about her directly. Since it only exempted a שליח בית דין, it seems she pays in every case.

steps.title: That is exactly what the ברייתא means
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that the ברייתא does mean this split. When she has no other way, her hand counts like a שליח בית דין, so she is exempt.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is indeed what it is saying: when is this said? When she could have saved him another way. But if she could not, her hand becomes like a messenger of the court, and she is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge. The words about the שליח בית דין are the split the questioner asked for.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The גמרא says the line 'excluding a שליח בית דין' already contains the split. When the woman has no other way, she herself counts like an agent of the court and is exempt. So the answer of Step 18 stands, and the ברייתא is no proof against acting on your own.

keyTerms.meaning: This is indeed what it is saying
Her hand becomes, her hand is treated as

steps.whatToRemember: The proof from 'וקצתה את כפה' fails. She pays only when she had a gentler option. When she had no other way, she is like a שליח בית דין and is פטור.

phrases.english: This is indeed what it is saying:
In what case are these words said?

phrases.aramaic: בְּשֶׁיְּכוֹלָה לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר,
phrases.english: Where she is able to save [him] by other means,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל אֵינָהּ יְכוֹלָה לְהַצִּיל עַל יְדֵי דָּבָר אַחֵר –
phrases.english: but where she is not able to save [him] by other means –
her hand becomes like a messenger of the court,
and she is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: הָכִי נָמֵי קָאָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 19 by rereading the end of the ברייתא.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Rereading the source: the end of the ברייתא is itself the split.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The שליח בית דין line is about a different person, so the woman always pays.
steps.terutzMaskana: The שליח בית דין line describes the woman herself when she has no other choice, so she is exempt then.

steps.title: New proof: the man who moved a public road off his field
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a משנה: if a public road ran through someone's field and he took it and gave the public a path on the side, what he gave stays theirs, and he does not get the old road back.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: if a public road passed through his field, and he took it and gave them a path on the side, what he gave, he gave, and his own does not come back to him.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new proof on the same question. Here it only quotes the משנה; how it proves the point comes right after.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A man fixed the problem himself by moving the public road to the edge of his field. The משנה says the new path now belongs to the public and he still cannot use the old road. The גמרא will use this to ask whether he was allowed to act on his own.

keyTerms.meaning: On the side, at the edge
Did not reach him, he does not get it

steps.confusionAlert: 'Did not reach him' means he loses both: the side path now belongs to the public, and he still cannot use the old road through his field.

phrases.english: Come and hear:
A case where a public road
passed through his field;
he took it, and gave them [a path] on the side –
what he gave, he gave,
and his own did not come to him.
phrases.notes: 'His own' is the old road through his field. He cannot take it back for himself.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: הֲרֵי שֶׁהָיְתָה דֶּרֶךְ הָרַבִּים עוֹבֶרֶת בְּתוֹךְ שָׂדֵהוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the proof from the woman fell away, the גמרא starts a new proof from a משנה.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a person may take the law into his own hands. The proof is set up here for the view of רב יהודה.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about a public road through a private field that the owner moved to the side.

steps.title: Why can't the owner just block the old road with a stick?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes the proof from the משנה. If a person may take the law into his own hands, the owner should be allowed to stand guard with a stick and keep the public off the old road.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if you say a person may take the law into his own hands, let the owner take a stick and sit there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא completes the proof it started in Step 21. It shows that the משנה seems to say a person may NOT take the law into his own hands.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה said the owner does not get the old road back. But if עביד איניש דינא לנפשיה were true, the owner could just block the old road himself, since he already gave the public a new path. The משנה does not allow that, so it seems a person may not act on his own.

keyTerms.meaning: A person may take the law into his own hands

phrases.english: And if you say
a person may take the law into his own hands,
let him take a stick and sit!
phrases.notes: He means: sit by the old road with a stick and keep people from walking through.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ עָבֵיד אִינִישׁ דִּינָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ, לִנְקוֹט פַּזְרָא וְלִיתֵיב
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof that began with the quote from the משנה in Step 21.
steps.raayaObject: That a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The משנה about a public road running through a field. The owner does not get the old road back, so he may not just block it himself.

steps.title: רב זביד: It is a rabbinic decree in case he gives a crooked path
steps.stepSummary: רב זביד, quoting רבא, says the משנה's rule is a גזירה. The חכמים feared the owner might give the public a crooked, worse path. So the משנה proves nothing about taking the law into one's own hands.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב זביד said in the name of רבא: It is a decree, in case he gives them a crooked path.
steps.whatsHappening: רב זביד pushes off the proof. He says the owner cannot block the road because of a rabbinic decree. It has nothing to do with the general rule about acting on your own.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This answer assumes רב נחמן's view, that by the basic law a person may take the law into his own hands. But the חכמים worried that owners would swap the road for a worse, winding path. So they made a גזירה against taking back the road at all. The משנה's rule comes from this decree, not from the basic law.

keyTerms.meaning: A rabbinic decree made to stop a possible problem

phrases.english: Rav Zevid said in the name of Rava:
It is a decree, in case he gives them
a crooked path.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב זְבִיד מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא: גְּזֵירָה שֶׁמָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in Steps 21–22.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The משנה's rule comes from a special rabbinic decree. It does not come from the general rule that one may not take the law into his own hands.

steps.title: רב משרשיא: The משנה is about a case where he really gave a crooked path
steps.stepSummary: רב משרשיא says the משנה is talking about a case where the owner actually gave a crooked path. That is why he cannot take the old road back.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב משרשיא said: The משנה is talking about where he gave them a crooked path.
steps.whatsHappening: רב משרשיא gives a second way to push off the proof. He narrows the case in the משנה to an owner who gave the public a worse, winding path.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב זביד needed a decree. רב משרשיא does not. He says the owner in the משנה really did give a bad path, so of course he loses. But if the owner gave a fair, straight path, he could block the old road himself. So the משנה does not prove that a person may never act on his own.

keyTerms.meaning: In a case where he gives them

phrases.english: Rav Mesharshiyya said:
It is where he gives them a crooked path.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב מְשַׁרְשְׁיָא אָמַר: בְּנוֹתֵן לָהֶם דֶּרֶךְ עֲקַלָּתוֹן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: A different way to push off the same proof, without needing a decree.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed the new path was fair. In the משנה's case the path was really crooked, so the owner loses for that reason.

steps.title: רב אשי: Any path on the side counts as crooked
steps.stepSummary: רב אשי says any path moved to the side is a crooked path. It is closer for some people and farther for others, so the owner can never fairly swap it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אשי said: Any path on the side is a crooked path. It is closer for this person and farther for that person.
steps.whatsHappening: רב אשי gives a third way to push off the proof. He says that by its nature, every side path is a worse path for someone.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב משרשיא limited the משנה to a case where the path really was crooked. רב אשי says every side path is like that, because moving the road helps some people and hurts others. So the owner always loses here because the swap is unfair. It has nothing to do with whether a person may take the law into his own hands.
steps.whatToRemember: The proof from the public road משנה is pushed off three ways. רב זביד says it is a rabbinic decree. רב משרשיא says the owner really gave a crooked path. רב אשי says every side path is crooked for someone. Either way, the משנה does not prove that a person may never take the law into his own hands.

phrases.english: Rav Ashi said:

phrases.aramaic: כֹּל מִן הַצַּד – דֶּרֶךְ עֲקַלָּתוֹן הוּא,
phrases.english: Any path on the side is a crooked path,
closer for this one and farther for that one.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָשֵׁי אָמַר: כֹּל מִן הַצַּד דֶּרֶךְ עֲקַלָּתוֹן הוּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Widens רב משרשיא's answer. Every side path, not just some, counts as crooked.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the משנה.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof assumed a side path could be a fair swap. In truth, any side path is worse for some people.

steps.title: Why can't the owner take back the path he gave?
steps.stepSummary: If the swap is never allowed, the owner should at least be able to cancel it and take back the side path he gave.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, why does he not get back what is his? Let him tell the public: take your old road and give me back my land!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב אשי's explanation from the last step. If the swap never works, why does the owner lose both pieces of land?
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב אשי said the owner can never fairly swap the road, because any new side path is crooked. The גמרא then asks: if the swap fails, the deal should simply be cancelled. The public should take back the old road and return the new path. Losing both pieces seems unfair.

keyTerms.meaning: If so, meaning if what you just said is true

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, אַמַּאי שֶׁלּוֹ לֹא הִגִּיעוֹ?
phrases.english: If so, why has what is his not come back to him?
phrases.notes: "What is his" is the side path he gave the public, which came from his own field.

phrases.english: Let him say to them: Take yours,
and give me mine!

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, אַמַּאי שֶׁלּוֹ לֹא הִגִּיעוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב אשי's explanation (step 25) by pointing to the second half of the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The משנה's ruling that the owner loses the side path he gave, as explained by רב אשי.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the swap is never valid, it should simply be cancelled and each side should get back its own land. The owner should not lose both.

steps.title: A path the public already uses may not be ruined
steps.stepSummary: The owner cannot take back the side path because of רב יהודה's rule: once the public uses a path, it may not be ruined.
steps.simpleTranslation: Because of רב יהודה, who said: a path that the public has taken hold of may not be ruined.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question by quoting רב יהודה. Once the public has started using a path, nobody may take it away from them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner loses the side path for a different reason than the swap. The public has already started walking on it, so it has become a public path. Taking it away would "ruin" a public path, and that is forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: A narrow path or strip along the edge of a field
The public has taken hold of it, meaning they began using it
It is forbidden to ruin it

steps.whyThisMatters: This rule explains why the owner loses both pieces of land. It is a rule about public rights. It says nothing about taking the law into one's own hands.

phrases.english: Because of the statement of רב יהודה,
as רב יהודה said:
A path that the public has taken hold of,
it is forbidden to ruin it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מִשּׁוּם דְּרַב יְהוּדָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 26.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings in an outside rule that explains the ruling.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Since the swap fails, the owner should get the side path back.
steps.terutzMaskana: He cannot get it back, because the public already uses it, and a public path may not be ruined (רב יהודה).

steps.title: A new proof: פאה taken from the wrong side
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: an owner left פאה on one side, and the poor took from another side. Both are פאה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Come and hear: an owner left פאה on one side of his field, and poor people came and took from a different side. Both this and that are פאה.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new attempt to prove whether a person may take the law into his own hands. Here it only quotes the ברייתא. The proof itself comes in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner set aside פאה in one spot, but the poor took produce from somewhere else. The ברייתא says both portions count as פאה. That seems to mean the poor can keep what they took from the wrong side.

keyTerms.meaning: The corner of the field left for the poor

phrases.english: Come and hear:

phrases.aramaic: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁהִנִּיחַ פֵּאָה מִצַּד אֶחָד,
phrases.english: An owner who left פאה on one side,
and poor people came and took from another side,
this and that are both פאה.

steps.triggerLanguage: תָּא שְׁמַע: בַּעַל הַבַּיִת שֶׁהִנִּיחַ פֵּאָה מִצַּד אֶחָד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The road proof has been pushed away, so the גמרא brings a new source.
steps.raayaObject: Whether a person may take the law into his own hands.

steps.title: The owner should be able to guard his field with a stick
steps.stepSummary: If a person may take the law into his own hands, the owner should stand guard with a stick and stop the poor. So why is the second portion פאה?
steps.simpleTranslation: If you say a person may take the law into his own hands, why are both portions פאה? Let him take a stick and sit there!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא draws the proof from the ברייתא. Since both portions are פאה, it seems the owner may not chase the poor away himself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the owner could protect his rights by himself, he could guard the wrong side and keep the poor away. The ברייתא calls both portions פאה, which seems to mean the poor win. That would show a person may not take the law into his own hands.

keyTerms.meaning: A person may take the law into his own hands

phrases.aramaic: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ עָבֵיד אִינִישׁ דִּינָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ,
phrases.english: And if you say a person may take the law into his own hands,
why are this and that both פאה?
Let him take a stick and sit!
phrases.notes: He means: let the owner sit on the wrong side with a stick and keep the poor away from it.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי אָמְרַתְּ עָבֵיד אִינִישׁ דִּינָא לְנַפְשֵׁיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof from the ברייתא quoted in step 28.
steps.raayaObject: That a person may not take the law into his own hands.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The ברייתא's ruling that both portions are פאה.

steps.title: Both are פאה only to free them from מעשר
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains that "both are פאה" only means both portions are free from מעשר. It does not mean the poor own both.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: What does "this and that are פאה" mean? To free them from מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא pushes away the proof. The ברייתא is not talking about who owns the produce. It is only saying that both portions are free from מעשר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The proof assumed that "both are פאה" means the poor get to keep both portions. רבא reads it differently: both portions get the פאה status of being free from מעשר. So the owner could still use a stick to guard the wrong side, and the proof falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: Tithes, the tenth of produce that must be separated

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think רבא is saying the second portion is not פאה at all. It is פאה in one sense, being free from מעשר. The ברייתא just isn't saying the poor have a right to take it.
steps.whatToRemember: The פאה proof is pushed away. The ברייתא is about freeing produce from מעשר, not about whether the owner may stop the poor himself.

phrases.english: רבא said:
What does "this and that are פאה" mean?
To exempt them from מעשר.
phrases.notes: פאה is free from מעשר. רבא means both portions get that same exemption.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי זֶה וָזֶה פֵּאָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the proof made in step 29.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole proof from the פאה ברייתא.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The proof read "both are פאה" as a rule about ownership. It is really a rule about being free from מעשר.

steps.title: A ברייתא shows that ownerless produce is free from מעשר
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא supports רבא with a ברייתא: one who makes his vineyard הפקר and then harvests it early must still give the poor their gifts, but he is exempt from מעשר.
steps.simpleTranslation: As it is taught in a ברייתא: A person who gives up ownership of his vineyard, then gets up early in the morning and harvests it himself, must still give פרט, עוללות, שכחה and פאה, but he is exempt from מעשר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to prove that רבא's reading is correct. The ברייתא shows that something which became ownerless is free from מעשר, even if the original owner takes it back.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the vineyard was הפקר, its produce is free from מעשר, and that stays true even though the owner harvested it himself. This matches רבא: the portion the owner first set aside as פאה became ownerless, so it stays free from מעשר even if he takes it back. That is all 'both are פאה' means. It does not mean the poor own what they took from the wrong side. So the earlier proof that a person may not take the law into his own hands falls away.

keyTerms.meaning: One who gives up ownership of his property and makes it free for anyone to take
Single grapes that fall during harvest; left for the poor
Small, poorly formed grape clusters; left for the poor
Clusters forgotten during harvest; left for the poor
The corner of the field or vineyard left for the poor
The tithe; does not apply to ownerless produce

steps.whatToRemember: Produce that was הפקר is free from מעשר even if the original owner later takes it. That is all 'both are פאה' meant, so the case of the פאה gives no proof about taking the law into your own hands.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up the two kinds of obligations. The gifts to the poor still apply to this harvester, but מעשר does not. The ברייתא is not saying he is exempt from everything.
steps.whyThisMatters: This closes the long side discussion that began with the question of whether a person may take the law into his own hands. The פאה ברייתא does not prove that he may not.

phrases.english: As it is taught: One who makes his vineyard ownerless,
and got up early in the morning and harvested it –
is obligated in fallen single grapes and in small clusters
and in forgotten clusters and in the corner,
and he is exempt from the tithe.

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּדְתַנְיָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports רבא's דחיה in step 30 with a ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: רבא's claim that 'both are פאה' only means both portions are free from מעשר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about one who makes his vineyard הפקר and then harvests it himself: he is exempt from מעשר.

steps.title: The משנה about a jug that breaks in the public street
steps.stepSummary: If a person's jug breaks in רשות הרבים and someone slips on the water or is hurt by the broken pieces, the owner is liable. רבי יהודה says he is liable only if he acted with intent.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: If a person's jug broke in the public area, and someone slipped in the water or was hurt by the broken pieces, the owner is liable. רבי יהודה says: if he had intent, he is liable; if he had no intent, he is exempt.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It gives the case of a jug that breaks in the street and hurts someone, and it brings a disagreement between the first opinion and רבי יהודה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first opinion says the jug owner pays for the damage whether the passerby slipped on the water or was hurt by the pieces. רבי יהודה adds a condition: only 'במתכוין,' with intent, does he pay. The משנה does not say here what kind of intent is meant, so the גמרא will need to explain it.

keyTerms.meaning: Our משנה; the start of a new משנה
The public domain, like a street where everyone walks

steps.confusionAlert: The two parts are separate dangers. One person slipped on the spilled water, and another was cut or hurt by the broken pieces.

phrases.english: MISHNA: If his jug broke in the public domain,
and someone slipped in the water
or was hurt by the shards – he is liable.
phrases.notes: 'He' here is the owner of the jug, not the one who got hurt.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yehuda says:
With intent – he is liable,
without intent – he is exempt.

steps.triggerLanguage: מַתְנִי׳ נִשְׁבְּרָה כַּדּוֹ בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new משנה after the side discussion ends.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The jug owner is liable when someone slips on the water or is hurt by the shards. רבי יהודה says he is liable only when he acted with intent.

steps.title: רב limits the liability to when the victim's clothes got dirty
steps.stepSummary: רב יהודה quotes רב: the משנה's ruling that the owner is liable applies only when the victim's clothes were dirtied by the water.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: רב יהודה said in the name of רב: The משנה taught that he is liable only when the victim's clothes got dirty from the water.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins explaining the משנה. רב narrows the case where the jug owner has to pay, and the statement continues past this point.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה sounded like the owner pays for everything that happens when someone slips. רב says no: the liability the משנה means is only for clothes dirtied by the water. The rest of his statement, which explains what he is excluding, comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: The discussion that explains the משנה
'They taught this only when...'; a phrase that narrows a ruling
His clothes (here); it can also mean his things or vessels

phrases.aramaic: גְּמָ׳ אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב:
phrases.english: GEMARA: Rav Yehuda said that Rav said:
They taught this only
when his clothes were soiled by the water,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב יְהוּדָה אָמַר רַב: לֹא שָׁנוּ אֶלָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts the גמרא's explanation of the משנה by narrowing when the jug owner is liable.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The jug owner is liable only for clothes dirtied by the water. The statement continues in the next lines.
